panels.figure_caption: Clinical manifestations of Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome (HPS)-3 patients. HPS-3 patients have variable hypopigmentation of skin and hair, as shown in probands 4 and 5 (B-II:8 and B-II:9, respectively) (A–B), and some show multiple ecchymoses due to a bleeding diathesis in HPS patients (proband 5) (C).
in_text_mentions: iagnosed at the Michelson Institute (Hadassah Medical Center, Jerusalem, Israel), and then referred to our clinic for molecular analysis. Of the five siblings, three are affected (probands 4, 5, and 6), including two brothers at the ages of 1.5 and 9 years and one sister at the age of 11. Two additional male siblings (7 and 4 years old) were reportedly healthy. The three affected siblings exhibit hypopigmentation of the skin and the hair, nystagmus, and a tendency to bleed. Of note, with time, an increase in pigmentation was observed in the older sister (clinical evaluation shown in Figure 1).

panels.figure_caption: Representative clinical findings in patients with causative HPS6 mutation. Figure shows a 5-year-old patient who carried compound heterozygous variants in HPS6 NM_024747, c.1021C>T (p.Gln341*) and c.1146_1147delTC (p.Gly382Glyfs*13). His hair color is brown (A) and iris color is brownish-black (B). Hypopigmentation was detected in the fundus (C) and foveal hypoplasia was shown in the OCT (D).
in_text_mentions: corrected visual acuity of the H1 proband was 0.5 (LogMAR) in each eye, 1.0 in both eyes of the proband H4, and not available in H2 and H3. Photophobia was observed in all (8/8) eyes, with the iris color being hazel, or brownish-black. Nystagmus was detected in all (4/4) patients and strabismus was found in one (1/4) patient. Fundus examination revealed fundus hypopigmentation and foveal hypoplasia in all (8/8) eyes. Ocular phenotypic characteristic of the patients with HPS were summarized in Table 2 and representative images of ocular manifestations in patients with HPS are shown in Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: 65-year-old HPS3 proband IV-3; panel A shows hair hypopigmentation/gray hair attributed to oculocutaneous albinism in HPS. B: Proband eye-position photo; in-text explicitly links to HPS proband esotropia. No vocabulary eye-movement key exists so captured as proposed esotropia/strabismus associated with albinotic visual pathway. C: Close-up iris photos labeled IV-3 left/right show transillumination defects typical of HPS oculocutaneous albinism; IV-4 at left is intra-panel comparator but panel demonstrates proband defect. D: Fundus of proband IV-3 left/right shows albinotic fundus with reduced retinal pigment / patchy lack of RPE, matching foveal hypoplasia with reduced retinal pigment. E: OCT of proband IV-3 shows absent foveal pit/structure, defining foveal hypoplasia/aplasia in HPS albinism.

in_text_mentions: The oral examination showed normal labial and buccal mucosa, normally hard and soft palates, and oropharynx. The oral hygiene was not good. The gums were red and swollen (Figure 1). The proband's periodontal status was examined using Florida probe® (Florida Probe Corp, Gainesville, FL). The DI reached 0–2, the CI reached 0–2, and BI reached 2–4. The percentage of positive BOP sites was 94%. The PPD was 1–9 mm, and PPD ≥ 3 mm accounted for 85%, among which PPD ≥ 5 mm accounted for 33%. The clinical attachment level (CAL) was 0~7 mm. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Panoramic radiograph of HPS type 2 proband showing moderate to severe alveolar bone resorption inconsistent with age 13 years; disease-focused title plus captioned manifestation supports HPS attribution. No vocabulary key covers periodontal bone loss, so captured as proposed findings. B: 3D volumetric CBCT of whole mouth from lateral view in same HPS proband showing alveolar bone loss. C: 3D volumetric CBCT frontal view of whole mouth in same HPS proband. D: 3D volumetric CBCT of whole mouth from opposite lateral direction in same HPS proband. E: Axial CBCT with arrows showing alveolar bones absorbed to root apex as captioned; severe loss in 13-year-old HPS type 2 proband. F: Coronal CBCT with arrow showing alveolar bone of tooth absorbed to root apex with almost no support. G: Sagittal CBCT with arrow showing alveolar bone loss to root apex.

in_text_mentions: Imaging examination (Cone-beam computed tomographic, CBCT) showed that most teeth have moderate to severe resorption of alveolar bone, which is inconsistent with age at 13 years. Alveolar bones of teeth #12, #11, and #26 were absorbed to the root apex and there was almost no alveolar bone support in the root (Figure 3).
